rationale: The preceding warning against an unbelieving heart, deception and failure to hold confidence supplies the immediate background to fearing that someone falls short of promised rest. The letter links these exhortations without identifying an unprinted individual as already excluded.

Both distinguish receiving a report from the faith response to it. Romans says not all obeyed the gospel and connects faith with hearing; Hebrews says the heard word did not benefit those not united by faith with the hearers. The source's actual plural union wording is retained.

Hebrews uses the Psalm's sworn refusal of entry into God's rest. The letter introduces believers entering rest and creation's works; the Psalm supplies the oath within its wilderness warning. The extra framing is not inserted into the Psalm.

Both say God rested on the seventh day from His works. Hebrews cites that rest statement; Genesis gives it within the creation account. The account's wording about completion is preserved separately and not normalized from another edition.

The repeated they-shall-not-enter-My-rest statement corresponds to the Greek-numbered Psalm's oath. This source unit repeats a citation in the argument; its native identity remains distinct from the earlier fuller4:3 use.

The earlier questions and conclusion connect failure to enter with disobedience and unbelief. The present inference says entry remains for some while former hearers failed through disobedience. The difference between those named reasons and groups remains as printed.

Hebrews reuses the Psalm's Today, hearing His voice and not hardening hearts. Its argument appoints a day and labels the saying in David; the actual Greek-numbered Psalm carries its own people-and-wilderness setting. No new critical authorship finding is supplied.

Acts places the ancestors' entrance with Joshua before the days of David. Hebrews contrasts Joshua with a later statement about another day in its rest argument. The comparison supplies the named historical frame without treating Joshua as Jesus Christ or defining every kind of rest.

Both connect God's people with Sabbath rest. Exodus commands the seventh-day rest and relates it to creation; Hebrews concludes that a Sabbath rest remains. The comparison does not turn Hebrews' conclusion into an identical weekly command or resolve every proposed timing of that rest.

God's resting from His works supplies the stated comparison for the one who enters His rest and rests from his own works. The unidentified one and those works in Hebrews are not given an unprinted exclusive identity or definition by the Genesis reference.

Diligence to enter rest is grounded in the earlier failure to enter through disobedience and unbelief. This is the specific prior pattern the same letter warns against, without deciding an individual's outcome beyond the stated exhortation.

Both connect God's word with a bladed weapon. Ephesians names the Spirit's sword; Hebrews describes living, active penetration and judgment of thoughts and intentions. The images do not supply an identical literal weapon or a complete anatomy theory.

The Psalm describes the Lord knowing the speaker's movements, thoughts and words. Hebrews states that no created thing is hidden before Him and adds giving account. The personal Psalm and all-creation accountability statement have different stated scopes.

Jesus as high priest passing through the heavens corresponds to Christ entering heaven itself to appear before God for us. The confession exhortation and the target's contrast with handmade holy places remain distinct.

Both connect high-priestly help with shared human weakness and testing. The earlier passage names likeness to brothers, mercy and help for the tested; this one explicitly adds testing in every way yet without sin. That no-sin clause is not supplied as wording of the earlier units.

Both describe bold and confident access in relation to Christ. Ephesians names access through faith in Him; Hebrews calls approach to grace's throne for mercy and timely help. The throne image and specific benefits remain in Hebrews.

Both describe a high priest's appointment to offer gifts and sacrifices. The later argument applies the requirement to this high priest; the present unit names appointment from and for people in God-related matters and for sins. The descriptions are not made identical in every scope.

Both relate priestly understanding of others to weakness. The ordinary high priest here is himself surrounded by weakness; the earlier Jesus statement expressly includes without sin. That qualification prevents simply transferring every ordinary priest's condition to Jesus.

relationship: priest offering for himself and others
rationale: Leviticus describes Aaron bringing the sin offering on his own behalf and for his household. Hebrews names the priest's obligation to offer for his own sins as well as the people's. The household and people formulations remain distinct, and no such sin is attributed to Jesus here.

God's instruction to bring Aaron and his sons near for priestly service supplies the named Aaron calling background. Hebrews contrasts taking the honor oneself with being called by God. The command's particular family list is not expanded into every later appointment.

Hebrews applies the Psalm's Thou-art-My-Son/today-begotten saying in its account of Christ not glorifying Himself as high priest. The Psalm's selected unit does not itself print the whole high-priest appointment explanation.

The priest-for-the-age according-to-Melchizedek-order formula corresponds to the Greek-numbered Psalm. Hebrews introduces it as another saying; the Psalm also records the Lord's oath and not repenting. Each introduction remains as supplied.

Both present Jesus in prayer while facing death. Matthew names sorrow, the cup and the Father's will; Hebrews names loud crying, tears, reverent fear and being heard by the One able to save out of death. The comparison does not define being heard as avoiding crucifixion or identify every petition with one scene.

Both connect the Son's obedience with suffering. Philippians names becoming obedient to death on a cross; Hebrews says He learned obedience from what He suffered. Neither is expanded with a claim of prior sinful disobedience.

Both connect perfecting with salvation in the suffering argument. The earlier unit names the pioneer of salvation perfected through sufferings; this one names the perfected One as source of eternal salvation for those obeying Him. The titles and recipient descriptions remain distinct.

Both identify the high priest according to Melchizedek's order. Hebrews6:20 expressly names Jesus entering as forerunner on our behalf;5:10 names God's designation. Their different predicates are kept without importing all of the later clause into the earlier unit.

relationship: much to say and hearer limitation
rationale: Both say there is much to say while naming a limitation in hearers. Jesus says the disciples cannot bear it now; Hebrews says explanation is hard because the readers have become slow to hear. Their hearers, reasons and unspecified teaching content are not made identical.

Both use milk and food in describing limited capacity to receive instruction. Corinthians names infants in Christ; Hebrews says those who ought to be teachers again need first elements and milk rather than solid food. The differing diagnoses and wording remain distinct.

Both contrast immaturity with mature reception of instruction. Ephesians names maturity in Christ and not remaining children carried by teaching; Hebrews names the milk-fed infant as inexperienced in righteousness's word. The food and wave images are not merged.

Both relate renewed or trained capacity to moral discernment. Romans names mind renewal to discern God's good, pleasing and perfect will; Hebrews names mature faculties trained through practice to distinguish good and evil. The specific processes and objects remain distinct.

relationship: advance from elementary teaching to maturity
rationale: Therefore carries forward the preceding milk/solid-food and infancy/maturity argument. The foundation language now names repentance and faith without requiring its foundations to be laid again. The link does not turn advancing to maturity into abandoning Christ, faith or repentance.

Two named foundational topics are resurrection of the dead and eternal judgment. Jesus speaks of those in tombs coming out to resurrection of life or judgment. The comparison addresses those two topics without defining the separate washings or laying-on-of-hands items.

The projected advance if God permits has a concrete parallel in Paul's hope to stay with the Corinthians if the Lord permits. The proposed actions differ; the shared conditional formula supplies no claim of common authorship.

Both warnings concern grave repudiation after receiving divine benefits. The later passage names knowledge of truth, the Son and insult to grace's Spirit; this one names enlightenment, heavenly gift and participation in the Holy Spirit. The precise conditions and implications are not flattened into one exhaustive interpretation.

relationship: tasting divine goodness and word nourishment
rationale: Both employ tasting and nourishment language in relation to divine goodness. Peter joins milk with growing and tasting the Lord's kindness; Hebrews names tasting God's good word and coming-age powers. Their objects and surrounding descriptions remain distinct.

relationship: repudiation and dishonor toward the Son
rationale: Both warnings portray grave dishonor toward the Son of God. The later passage speaks of trampling Him and treating covenant blood as common; this unit speaks of falling away and crucifying Him again for themselves and public disgrace. The different images are not asserted as the same literal physical act.

Both use rain watering land and producing useful growth. Isaiah applies the seed-and-bread illustration to God's effective word; Hebrews names cultivated land sharing blessing through useful vegetation. The distinct applications are preserved.

Both connect land, thorns or thistles, and a curse. Genesis gives the ground's curse in Adam's judgment; Hebrews contrasts rejected thorn-bearing land with useful growth and adds burning. That burning is not inserted into Genesis's wording.

The later we-are-not-of-shrinking-back-but-faith statement parallels confidence in better things accompanying the readers' salvation here. Both reassure within a warning discourse. The actual pronouns and statements are retained without making an unqualified judgment about every warned person.

Both explicitly name service to the saints. Corinthians describes eager participation in that ministry; Hebrews names the readers' continuing service as love toward God's name that He will not unjustly forget. The collection's particulars are not assigned to the Hebrews readers.

Both connect assurance with continuing to the end. Hebrews3:14 names holding the beginning of confidence firm as Christ's partners;6:11 desires each reader's diligence toward full assurance of hope. Their precise exhortation and condition remain distinct.

relationship: Abraham as patience and promise example
rationale: The following named Abraham example gives concrete content to imitating those who inherit through faith and patience. It describes God's promise and oath and his patient obtaining. The example is not made an exhaustive account of all promised outcomes.

Genesis records the Lord's by-Myself-I-have-sworn declaration to Abraham. Hebrews explicitly reasons that God swore by Himself because none was greater. The target does not independently repeat that whole explanatory reasoning.

Both give emphatic blessing and multiplication language in the Abraham promise. Genesis expands the promise through his seed and its comparison with stars and sand; Hebrews gives its shorter blessing-you/multiplying-you form. The objects and additional clauses remain distinct.

Both present Abraham's sustained trust in God's promise. Romans names hope against hope and conviction that God can perform what He promised; Hebrews says he waited patiently and obtained the promise. The descriptions do not identify every promised outcome or impose an unprinted oath-to-birth chronology.

relationship: oath confirming a disputed custody matter
rationale: Exodus specifies an oath by God between parties about entrusted property, accepted by the owner. This supplies a concrete case of an oath settling a dispute as Hebrews describes. The particular legal rule is not made a complete definition of every human oath.

The Lord's oath and not repenting in the priestly Psalm give a specific parallel to God's oath showing unchanging purpose. Hebrews here concerns heirs of the Abraham promise; the Psalm concerns priesthood. The two oath occasions are not made identical.

relationship: God cannot lie and promised hope
rationale: Both explicitly connect hope or promise with God's inability to lie. Titus names eternal life's hope promised before the ages; Hebrews names two unchangeable things and encouragement to hold the hope set before refugees. Their promise settings and images remain distinct.

The hope-anchor entering behind the veil is related to bold entry by Jesus' blood through the veil in the later argument. The later unit explicitly names His flesh as its veil explanation; that wording is not silently inserted into6:19 or used to make its anchor a literal boat fitting.

Hebrews names Jesus as forerunner and high priest according to Melchizedek's order for the age. The Psalm supplies the priest-for-the-age/order formula but does not itself print Jesus' name or the entry-as-forerunner statement. The application and additional predicate remain in Hebrews.
